title: Time-Based Key-Value Store — map of key→sorted(timestamp, value), binary search.
shortTitle: Time-Based Key-Value Store — map of key to sorted (timestamp, value) with binary search

s1_definition.profdef: A Time-Based Key-Value Store lets you set a value for a key at a given timestamp and later get the value that was current at or before a query timestamp. It is implemented as a hash map from each key to a list of timestamp-value pairs kept in increasing timestamp order, and a get performs a binary search over that list to find the largest timestamp not exceeding the query time.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India records the published interest rate for each product every time it changes, each change stamped with the date and time. Later, an auditor asks "what was the interest rate for savings as of last Tuesday noon." The clerk flips to the savings product's history, which is sorted by time, and quickly jumps to the latest entry that is on or before last Tuesday noon rather than reading the whole history.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep each key's history sorted by time and binary-search for the latest entry at or before the query timestamp to answer point-in-time lookups fast.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Time-Based Key-Value Store lets you set a value for a key at a given timestamp and later get the value that was current at or before a query timestamp. It is implemented as a hash map from each key to a list of timestamp-value pairs kept in increasing timestamp order, and a get performs a binary search over that list to find the largest timestamp not exceeding the query time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India records the published interest rate for each product every time it changes, each change stamped with the date and time. Later, an auditor asks "what was the interest rate for savings as of last Tuesday noon." The clerk flips to the savings product's history, which is sorted by time, and quickly jumps to the latest entry that is on or before last Tuesday noon rather than reading the whole history.

**One line to remember:** Keep each key's history sorted by time and binary-search for the latest entry at or before the query timestamp to answer point-in-time lookups fast.

sections.s2_technical:
The store maps each key to an ordered list of entries, where each entry holds a timestamp and the value set at that timestamp. The `set(key, value, timestamp)` operation appends a new entry to that key's list. In the common interview framing, timestamps for a key arrive in strictly increasing order, so appending keeps the list sorted automatically; if they can arrive out of order, you would insert into the correct position or sort, but the classic version assumes increasing timestamps.

The `get(key, timestamp)` operation must return the value whose timestamp is the largest one that is still less than or equal to the query timestamp. Because the list is sorted by timestamp, we binary-search for that boundary. We keep a low and high pointer and look for the rightmost entry whose timestamp does not exceed the query. If every stored timestamp is greater than the query, there is no valid value and we return an empty result.

The binary search runs in O(log n) for a key with n entries, and set runs in O(1) amortized when appending. The space is proportional to the total number of set calls. A senior nuance is the exact binary-search condition: we are performing a "floor" search, so when the midpoint timestamp is less than or equal to the query we record it as a candidate and move right to seek an even later valid one, and when it exceeds the query we move left. Getting this boundary logic right is the crux; an off-by-one here returns the wrong historical value.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India must answer "what interest rate applied to this product at this exact moment" for dispute resolution and audits. Rates change over time, and the bank keeps the full history, so a lookup is really a point-in-time query against a time-ordered history.

This is exactly how a Time-Based Key-Value Store works. We fetch the value that was in force at or before the asked timestamp.

Problem 2 — Histories can be long, so scanning every historical rate for every query would be too slow when auditors run thousands of point-in-time checks.

This is exactly why each key's history is sorted by timestamp and we binary-search it, turning a long scan into a logarithmic jump.

The code will have an `Entry` holder, a `TimeMap` class with `set` and `get` using binary search, and a runnable demo that records several rate changes for a product and queries the rate at various past timestamps with logging.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three rate changes for SAVINGS_RATE at timestamps 10, 20, and 35, then four point-in-time queries.

Step 1: The three `set` calls append entries to the SAVINGS_RATE list in increasing timestamp order, giving a sorted history of (10, "350"), (20, "400"), (35, "425").

Step 2: `get("SAVINGS_RATE", 5)` binary-searches for the largest timestamp at most 5. The first entry has timestamp 10, which exceeds 5, so no candidate is ever recorded and the result is the empty string, meaning no rate was in force yet.

Step 3: `get("SAVINGS_RATE", 10)` finds the entry at timestamp 10 exactly, records "350" as a candidate, then searches right but finds nothing smaller or equal beyond it, so it returns "350".

Step 4: `get("SAVINGS_RATE", 25)` finds timestamp 20 is at most 25, records "400", then checks timestamp 35 which exceeds 25, so it returns "400". `get("SAVINGS_RATE", 99)` records progressively later candidates up to timestamp 35 and returns "425".

Final output:

```
2026-10-27 13:10:00 INFO    rate at t=5  -> 
2026-10-27 13:10:00 INFO    rate at t=10 -> 350
2026-10-27 13:10:00 INFO    rate at t=25 -> 400
2026-10-27 13:10:00 INFO    rate at t=99 -> 425
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  set SAVINGS_RATE 350@10, 400@20, 425@35
    │ store: { SAVINGS_RATE : [(10,350),(20,400),(35,425)] }  (sorted by time)
    ▼
  get(SAVINGS_RATE, 25)
    │ binary search floor(25)
    │ mid=1 (20<=25) → candidate 400, low=2
    │ mid=2 (35>25)  → high=1 → stop
    ▼
  return "400"

  get(.,5) → first ts 10 > 5 → "" (no rate yet)
  get(.,99) → floor = 35 → "425"
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — TimeMap ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns / Principles ───────────────────────────┐
  │  HashMap<key, sorted List<Entry>> + binary floor search  │
  │  S (SOLID): TimeMap only stores time-versioned values    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐       ┌──────────────────┐
  │            TimeMap            │ holds │      Entry       │
  │  - store: Map<String,         │◆─────▶│  + timestamp:int │
  │        List<Entry>>           │       │  + value: String │
  │  ─────────────────────────────│       └──────────────────┘
  │  + set(key,value,ts): void    │  O(1) amortized
  │  + get(key, ts): String       │  O(log n) floor search
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  Contract for get(key, ts):
    Post: returns value of largest stored ts <= query ts, else ""
    Boundary: ts<=query → record & go right; ts>query → go left
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A Time-Based Key-Value Store lets me set a value for a key at a specific timestamp and later ask for the value that was in force at or before a query timestamp. It is a point-in-time lookup over a history, and I implement it as a hash map from each key to a list of timestamp-value pairs kept in increasing timestamp order, with the get operation using binary search over that list.

The set operation appends a new timestamp-value pair to the key's list. In the standard framing the timestamps for a key arrive in increasing order, so appending keeps the list sorted for free; if they could arrive out of order I would insert at the correct position instead. The get operation is where the real work is: I need the value whose timestamp is the largest one still less than or equal to the query, which is a floor search. I binary-search with a low and a high pointer, and whenever the midpoint timestamp is at most the query I record that value as a candidate and move right to look for an even later valid entry, and whenever it exceeds the query I move left. If every stored timestamp is greater than the query, I return an empty result because no value existed yet.

The subtle part is the floor boundary logic, because an off-by-one there returns the wrong historical value, which in a bank audit is unacceptable. Set is amortized constant time and get is logarithmic in the number of entries for that key.

In my project at National Bank of India, we had to answer what interest rate applied to a product at an exact moment for dispute resolution, and rates changed over time with the full history retained. Modeling each product's rate history as a time-sorted list and binary-searching it turned what would have been a long scan per query into a fast logarithmic jump, which kept auditor tooling responsive even when thousands of point-in-time checks ran against long histories.
